figure: FIGURE 3.4 (Dense vs MoE parameter allocation and KV cache behavior)
issue: Caption's active-parameter arithmetic does not close: it states '~12.8B is active per token: the always-on attention/shared weights (~1.4B) plus the two routed experts (11.2B + 5.7B)'. 1.4 + 11.2 + 5.7 = 18.3B, not 12.8B. The figure itself says 'active experts = 23 GB resident (2 x 11.4)' = 11.4B routed params, so the correct decomposition is 1.4 + 5.7 + 5.7 = 12.8B. The '11.2B' term is wrong (it appears to be a stray 2 x 5.6 or a mis-keyed '5.7').
evidence: Figure legend: 'active experts = 23 GB resident (2 x 11.4)' and '1 expert = 5.78 params = 11.4 GB (FP16)'. 23 GB / 2 bytes = 11.5B params for two experts, i.e. 5.7B each. Caption's own total (12.8B) is consistent with 1.4 + 2 x 5.7, and inconsistent with its printed breakdown.
acceptance_test: Caption reads '~12.8B is active per token: the always-on attention/shared weights (~1.4B) plus the two routed experts (5.7B + 5.7B)', and the three terms sum to 12.8B. A reviewer recomputing the sum from the printed caption obtains 12.8B exactly.

issue: Internal numeric inconsistency in the per-expert line: 5.78B params at FP16 (2 bytes/param) = 11.56 GB, not 11.4 GB. Further, 8 x 5.78B = 46.24B params = 92.5 GB, which does not match the figure's '91 GB experts' (8 x 11.4 GB = 91.2 GB, implying 5.7B params/expert). One of the two numbers (5.78 or 11.4/91) is wrong.
evidence: Figure text: '1 expert = 5.78 params = 11.4 GB (FP16)'; 'MoE total resident = 94 GB = 91 GB experts + 3 GB always-on'; 'inactive experts = 68 GB (6 x 11.4)'; 'active experts = 23 GB resident (2 x 11.4)'. 91/8 = 11.375 GB/expert = 5.69B params/expert.
acceptance_test: Either the line reads '1 expert = 5.7B params = 11.4 GB (FP16)' with 8 x 5.7B x 2 B = 91.2 GB, or it reads '5.78B params = 11.56 GB' with the totals updated to 92.5 GB experts / 95.5 GB total. All three printed quantities (per-expert GB, expert subtotal, total resident) must be mutually consistent to within the stated rounding.

figure: FIGURE 3.4 (KV panels: 'Dense KV = 12 GB' vs 'MoE KV = 0.6 GB')
issue: The two KV figures are only comparable if they refer to the same token count, but neither the figure nor the caption states the context length. The caption asserts 'the KV bytes per token follow each model's own attention shape' without giving bytes/token or the token count, so the 20x ratio (12 GB vs 0.6 GB) is presented as an unexplained number. The reader cannot verify the comparison, and the caption's claim that routing does not change KV is the chapter's key point.
evidence: Recomputation at 8-bit KV: dense (80 layers, hidden 8192, full MHA) = 2 x 80 x 8192 x 1 B = 1.31 MB/token; MoE (32 layers, hidden 4096, 8 KV heads x 128 = 1024 KV dim) = 2 x 32 x 1024 x 1 B = 64 KB/token. 12 GB / 1.31 MB = ~9.2K tokens; 0.6 GB / 64 KB = ~9.8K tokens. Both are consistent with a ~9.2K-token context, but that number appears nowhere.
acceptance_test: The figure states the shared context length (e.g. 'at 9.2K tokens') and the per-token KV bytes for each shape (1.31 MB/token dense, 64 KB/token MoE), so that 12 GB and 0.6 GB can be independently recomputed from the printed values.

figure: FIGURE 3.4 (dense 70B panel: 4x5 grid of blue squares)
issue: The dense-model grid is a decorative 20-square block with no stated meaning (no 'not to scale' note, unlike the MoE side), while the MoE grid encodes per-expert identity and active/inactive state. A reader may infer that the dense grid encodes something countable (e.g. 20 units of parameter mass) that it does not.
evidence: Caption applies 'not shown to scale' only to the MoE expert set ('~94 GB, not shown to scale'). The dense grid has 20 identical squares with no legend entry.
acceptance_test: Either add a 'not to scale' note to the dense grid, or replace it with a single labeled block ('140 GB resident & active') so that only the MoE grid carries per-unit encoding.

issue: The figure asserts a specific execution model for Wan2.2 A14B ('Not two experts within one forward'; 'Only high-noise expert runs' / 'Only low-noise expert runs'), i.e. that the two experts run in separate forward passes selected by denoising stage. This is a first-party architectural claim about a specific released model and must be sourced; the caption's Scope line ('official rounded counts ... not an inferred per-expert split') explicitly disclaims the very per-expert split the figure draws.
evidence: Figure text: 'Denoising schedule progresses / Not two experts within one forward'; stage boxes 'Only high-noise expert runs' and 'Only low-noise expert runs'. Caption: 'Scope: official rounded counts (about 27B total, about 14B active), not an inferred per-expert split; schematic (no step counts).' The figure's stage boxes ARE a per-expert split.
acceptance_test: Either (a) the caption's Scope line is rewritten to state that the per-expert stage assignment is schematic/illustrative and is not an official statement, or (b) the caption cites the first-party source for the stage-wise expert routing and the Scope line no longer disclaims a per-expert split. The two statements must not conflict.

issue: The diagram mixes two connector semantics with no legend: dashed blue arrows (checkpoint -> stage, i.e. 'which checkpoint is loaded/selected') and a solid black arrow (high-noise stage -> low-noise stage, i.e. temporal progression of the denoising schedule). The reader must guess which arrow means 'selection' and which means 'time'.
evidence: Rendered page shows two dashed blue vertical arrows from the checkpoint boxes and one solid horizontal black arrow between the stage boxes; no key is provided in figure or caption.
acceptance_test: Add a one-line key to the figure (or caption) distinguishing dashed = checkpoint selection, solid = denoising-schedule progression.

issue: Roughly the top quarter of the printed page is empty before the figure begins, and the figure block is then followed by a large gap before the caption. The page reads as under-filled relative to the rest of the chapter.
evidence: Rendered page 63: content starts at approximately 25% down the page; the figure's own title line is the first ink.
acceptance_test: The figure is floated to the top of the page (or the preceding text is allowed to fill the page) so that no more than ~10% of the page height is blank above the first element.

issue: Active/inactive expert state in the MoE grid is encoded by fill color (orange vs gray) with no shape or hatch difference. In grayscale the orange and gray squares differ only in luminance, and the dense-model blue squares are a third luminance class; a reader printing in grayscale must rely on the E1-E8 labels plus the legend to decode state.
evidence: Rendered page 67: MoE grid uses orange fill for E1/E4, light gray for E2/E3/E5/E6/E7/E8, blue for the dense grid; no pattern or outline differentiation.
acceptance_test: Active experts carry a distinct outline or hatch in addition to fill, so that active/inactive state survives grayscale reproduction and color-vision deficiency.

issue: The figure introduces a second, competing taxonomy that contradicts the one established one chapter earlier, and the relationship between the two is never stated. FIG 4.1 (PDF 93 / printed 73) presents 'the six workload dimensions' (Quality requirements; Traffic/concurrency; Token profile; Latency SLO; Economic constraints; Operational constraints) as the book's workload-characterization vocabulary. FIG 5.1's top box, also labelled 'Workload characterization', lists only three items: 'tokens · cost · SLO'. A reader who has just absorbed the six-dimension frame will read the three-item box as a contradiction (or, worse, as a silent narrowing of the framework). Separately, the caption calls the five boxes 'the model-selection dimensions', introducing a third label for what are visibly derived from the Chapter 4 dimensions (latency -> Latency SLO; KV cache -> Token profile; S/Tok -> Economic constraints). The book never says whether the five surfaces are a subset of the six dimensions, a refinement of them, or an orthogonal axis.
evidence: Page 73 figure header 'WORKLOAD DIMENSION' with six rows; caption: 'The six workload dimensions and the architectural decision each one drives'. Page 92 figure box 1: 'Workload characterization' / 'tokens · cost · SLO'; caption: 'The five surfaces are the model-selection dimensions'. No cross-reference to Chapter 4 or to FIG 4.1 appears on page 92.
acceptance_test: Either (a) relabel the top box 'Workload characterization (subset shown: tokens · cost · SLO)' and add a caption clause stating that only the dimensions that bind model selection are drawn, or (b) replace the three items with the Chapter 4 vocabulary. In addition, add one caption sentence defining the relation between the six workload dimensions and the five selection surfaces (e.g. 'the five surfaces are the subset of the six dimensions that constrain model choice; the remaining dimension, Operational constraints, is out of scope for this figure'). Verify that a reader who has read p. 73 can state whether the five surfaces are a subset, a refinement, or a separate axis.

issue: The abbreviation 'S/Tok' in the 'Five selection surfaces' box is undefined on the page and has two plausible readings that are not equivalent, one of which duplicates an adjacent term. Reading A: 'seconds per token' (i.e. TPOT / decode latency), which duplicates the adjacent surface 'latency'. Reading B: '$ per token' (cost per token), which duplicates the 'cost' item in the box immediately above ('tokens · cost · SLO'). Because the figure is the reader's first encounter with the token, and because the caption's whole argument is that the five surfaces are a distinct set, an ambiguous member of that set weakens the figure's central claim. The book elsewhere uses 'TPOT' for time-per-output-token, so a reader is likely to reach for that reading and then find the surface list redundant.
evidence: Figure box 2 sub-label: 'quality · latency · KV cache · S/Tok · retrieve-vs-generate'. Figure box 1 sub-label: 'tokens · cost · SLO'. Caption: 'The five surfaces are the model-selection dimensions'. No expansion of 'S/Tok' appears in the caption, the figure, or the visible page text.
acceptance_test: Replace 'S/Tok' with an unambiguous phrase ('cost per token' or 'seconds per output token'), or define the abbreviation in the caption and in the glossary. Confirm that the resulting five-item list contains no item that restates 'latency' or 'cost' from the box above. Verify against the Chapter 5 body text that the chosen expansion matches the term the chapter actually uses.

issue: The word 'quality' denotes two different things inside one figure, and the caption asserts they are distinct without disambiguating them. 'quality' is one of the five selection surfaces in the drawn box; 'retrieval quality' and 'final answer quality' are two of the five end-to-end evaluation gates listed in the caption. The caption's claim that the surfaces are 'deliberately distinct from the end-to-end evaluation gates' is therefore made using an identical word for one surface and two gates, with no clause saying which 'quality' the surface refers to. A reader can plausibly conclude that the 'quality' surface IS the retrieval-quality gate, which is precisely the confusion the caption says it is excluding.
evidence: Figure box 2 sub-label: 'quality · latency · KV cache · S/Tok · retrieve-vs-generate'. Caption: 'they are deliberately distinct from the end-to-end evaluation gates (retrieval quality, reranking, embedding recall, grounding, and final answer quality) that a RAG system must also pass'.
acceptance_test: Rename the surface so it cannot collide with a gate name (e.g. 'answer-quality bar' or 'quality requirement'), and/or add a caption clause naming which quality each refers to. Verify that no reader can map the surface 'quality' onto either 'retrieval quality' or 'final answer quality' without re-reading the caption.

issue: The drawing implies that all five selection surfaces apply to both legs, but the surfaces are not leg-symmetric. A single 'Five selection surfaces' box fans out through two arrows labelled 'split' to 'Retrieval leg' and 'Generation leg', which reads as 'these five surfaces are then evaluated for each leg'. Two of the five are generation-leg concepts: an embedding model has no autoregressive KV cache, and it has no per-token decode cost of the kind 'S/Tok' denotes. The figure therefore permits the inference that the embedding model has a KV cache, which is a substantive architectural error rather than a stylistic one.
evidence: Figure: 'Five selection surfaces' -> two arrows labelled 'split' -> 'Retrieval leg' (embedding · 768-dim) and 'Generation leg' (70B FP16 · serving). Surface list includes 'KV cache' and 'S/Tok'. Caption describes the surfaces as applying to 'model selection' generally and does not qualify which surfaces bind which leg.
acceptance_test: Annotate the two split arrows with the surfaces that bind each leg (e.g. 'quality · latency · cost/token' for retrieval; 'quality · latency · KV cache · cost/token' for generation), or add a caption sentence stating that the surfaces are evaluated per leg and that KV cache and per-token decode cost apply only to the generation leg. Verify that no reader concludes the embedding model holds a KV cache.

figure: FIGURE 4.1 (Six-dimension workload characterization mapped to architectural decisions)
issue: The caption contradicts itself about the cardinality of the mapping. The first paragraph states that 'The arrows are non-exclusive: in practice a dimension often influences several decisions at once'. The second paragraph then describes the figure as 'The six workload dimensions and the architectural decision each one drives' — singular 'the architectural decision', 'each one drives' — which asserts exactly the one-to-one mapping the first paragraph disclaims. The figure's own note ('primary mapping shown; cross-influences omitted') is consistent with the first paragraph, so the second paragraph is the outlier. The result is that the caption simultaneously teaches and un-teaches the same point in consecutive paragraphs.
evidence: Caption paragraph 1: 'Each arrow means the dimension constrains/informs the corresponding architectural choice - it is a heuristic influence, not a deterministic one-to-one mapping. The arrows are non-exclusive: in practice a dimension often influences several decisions at once'. Caption paragraph 2: 'The six workload dimensions and the architectural decision each one drives: Quality requirements -> model size/type; ...'.
acceptance_test: Rewrite paragraph 2 to use non-exclusive language, e.g. 'The six workload dimensions and the primary architectural decision each one informs: ...', and confirm that no sentence in the caption asserts a one-to-one mapping. Verify the revised caption against the figure note 'primary mapping shown; cross-influences omitted (see caption)'.

issue: The caption's parenthetical is missing a separator and reads as a run-on: 'two legs (retrieval/embedding generation/70B)'. The intended reading is '(retrieval/embedding, generation/70B)', matching the drawn boxes 'Retrieval leg - embedding · 768-dim' and 'Generation leg - 70B FP16 · serving'. As printed, 'embedding generation' can be parsed as a single phrase, which is confusing in a figure whose whole point is that the two legs are distinct.
evidence: Caption: 'Model selection for RAG workload - five selection surfaces -> two legs (retrieval/embedding generation/70B) -> the system decision.'
acceptance_test: Render as 'two legs (retrieval/embedding, generation/70B)'. Verify the parenthetical maps one-to-one onto the two drawn leg boxes.

issue: The 'Generation leg' box is drawn with a visibly heavier and darker border than every other box in the figure (including its sibling 'Retrieval leg'). The emphasis is unexplained by the caption or the prose. It matters more than a cosmetic inconsistency because, in grayscale, all five box fills fall in a narrow light band (green, pink, purple, tan, blue-gray all convert to roughly 78-82% gray), so the border weight is the only visual differentiator between the two legs once color is removed. An unexplained emphasis cue that survives grayscale is a semantic claim the reader cannot decode.
evidence: Rendered page 92: 'Generation leg' box outline is thicker and darker than 'Retrieval leg', 'Workload characterization', 'Five selection surfaces', and 'RAG system decision'. No caption clause refers to emphasis, the canonical model, or the 70B leg being the subject of the chapter.
acceptance_test: Normalize all five box borders to the same weight and color, or state the reason for the emphasis in the caption (e.g. 'the generation leg is the subject of this chapter'). Verify that in a grayscale rendering the two legs are distinguished by their labels and by nothing else.

issue: The five selection surfaces are drawn as a single run-on line of dot-separated words ('quality · latency · KV cache · S/Tok · retrieve-vs-generate'), which renders them as an undifferentiated list. The caption's argument depends on the reader being able to count and individuate the five surfaces and hold them apart from the five evaluation gates, but the drawing provides no visual structure that supports that count. Five discrete chips (or a two-column mini-list) would make the 'five' verifiable at a glance and would also make the leg-specific applicability (see FIG-5.1-03) expressible.
evidence: Figure box 2 sub-label is one continuous line of five items; caption: 'The five surfaces are the model-selection dimensions; they are deliberately distinct from the end-to-end evaluation gates'.
acceptance_test: Render the five surfaces as five visually discrete items. Verify that a reader can count five without reading the caption, and that the count matches the caption's enumeration.

issue: The diagram's structure reads as two parallel legs converging on a decision, with no depiction of the retrieved context entering the generation leg. The 'context' arrow runs from 'Retrieval leg' directly to 'RAG system decision', bypassing 'Generation leg'. The caption frames the figure as a selection map rather than a pipeline, which makes the parallel reading defensible, but the drawing alone permits the inference that the two legs are independent selections whose outputs are combined only at the end - i.e. that the retrieved context is not an input to generation. That is the defining structural property of RAG and the figure is the natural place a reader would look for it.
evidence: Figure: arrow labelled 'context' from 'Retrieval leg' to 'RAG system decision'; arrow labelled 'answer' from 'Generation leg' to 'RAG system decision'; no arrow from 'Retrieval leg' to 'Generation leg'. Caption: '...this figure is a selection map, not an evaluation pipeline.'
acceptance_test: Either route the 'context' arrow into the 'Generation leg' box (with 'answer' continuing to the system decision), or add a caption clause: 'the two legs are selected in parallel; the retrieved context is supplied to the generation leg at serving time (not shown)'. Verify that no reader concludes the legs are independent of one another.

figure: FIGURE 4.1 (Six-dimension workload characterization mapped to architectural decisions)
issue: The row 'Traffic / concurrency' -> 'concurrency & batching' uses the word 'concurrency' on both sides of the arrow, which reads as circular: concurrency determines concurrency. The intended distinction is between observed/offered load and the serving-side concurrency target and batching policy. The same row also conflates two different quantities (an arrival rate and a concurrency level) in one label, whereas the other five rows each name one dimension.
evidence: Figure row 2: left box 'Traffic / concurrency', right box 'concurrency & batching'. Caption: 'Traffic/concurrency -> concurrency & batching'.
acceptance_test: Relabel the left box to name the input unambiguously (e.g. 'Offered load / arrival rate') and the right box to name the decision (e.g. 'concurrency target & batching policy'). Verify that no row of the figure reads as self-referential.

figure: FIGURE 4.1 (Six-dimension workload characterization mapped to architectural decisions)
issue: The caption's second paragraph is a verbatim restatement of the figure's six drawn mappings, adding no information beyond what the drawing already shows, while the first paragraph (which does carry the argument) is the one a reader is most likely to skim. The result is that the caption's intellectual content is diluted by a legend that duplicates the visual. If the restatement is retained for accessibility, it should be compressed to a single sentence; otherwise the caption should lead with the semantics of the arrows and the non-exclusivity caveat.
evidence: Caption paragraph 2 lists all six mappings in the same order and with the same wording as the drawn boxes ('Quality requirements -> model size/type; Traffic/concurrency -> concurrency & batching; Token profile -> KV cache size & prefill demand; Latency SLO -> TTFT/TPOT & batch window; Economic constraints -> host count & cost ceiling; Operational constraints -> multi-region vs. single-region deployment').
acceptance_test: Compress the restatement to one sentence or remove it, keeping the arrow-semantics and non-exclusivity sentences. Confirm the figure remains self-explanatory without the restatement and that the caption still carries the non-exclusivity caveat.

figure: FIGURE 4.1 (Six-dimension workload characterization mapped to architectural decisions)
issue: In-figure annotation type sizes are at or near the legibility floor and should be measured before release. The italic note 'primary mapping shown; cross-influences omitted (see caption)' and, on page 92, the box sub-labels ('tokens · cost · SLO'; 'quality · latency · KV cache · S/Tok · retrieve-vs-generate'; 'embedding · 768-dim'; '70B FP16 · serving'; 'base + RAG + guardrails') and the arrow labels ('drives', 'split', 'context', 'answer') are all set noticeably smaller than the bold box titles. At the 150 dpi render they are readable but thin, and the longest sub-label on page 92 is the most at risk. These are in-text annotations within figures, so the 8 pt floor applies to them.
evidence: Rendered pages 93 and 112: annotation text is visibly smaller than the bold box titles; the page-92 sub-label 'quality · latency · KV cache · S/Tok · retrieve-vs-generate' is the longest single-line annotation in the batch.
acceptance_test: Measure rendered glyph heights for every in-figure annotation at 100% print scale on both pages; all must be >= 8 pt, and the longest sub-label must not wrap, shrink, or clip. Re-render at 150 dpi and confirm the note on p. 73 and the five sub-labels on p. 92 remain legible without magnification.

figure: FIGURE 4.1 and FIGURE 5.1 (both pages are figure-only pages)
issue: Both pages in this batch are float pages whose lower region is empty: on printed page 73 roughly the bottom 18% of the page below the caption is blank, and on printed page 92 roughly the bottom 22%. The result is two consecutive pages with a large dead band at the foot, which reads as an unfinished layout rather than a deliberate figure page. Because the two pages are adjacent in the same chapter sequence, the effect compounds.
evidence: Rendered PDF 93 / printed 73: caption ends at approximately 82% of page height, remainder blank. Rendered PDF 112 / printed 92: caption ends at approximately 78% of page height, remainder blank. No body text follows either caption on the page.
acceptance_test: Reflow so that the figure plus caption shares a page with the following body text, or vertically center the float block so the trailing band is distributed. Verify that the reflow introduces no widow/orphan, no stranded heading, and no caption separated from its figure.
